worked_example.stem: In a town, \(30\%\) of the households have solar panels. Of the households with solar panels, \(80\%\) have an electric water heater. Of the households without solar panels, \(20\%\) have an electric water heater. If a household in the town that has an electric water heater is selected at random, what is the probability that it has solar panels?
walkthrough: Imagine 1,000 households: 300 with solar panels and 700 without.
With an electric water heater: \(0.8 \times 300 = 240\) with panels and \(0.2 \times 700 = 140\) without, so 380 in all.
The condition is \"has an electric water heater\", so divide by 380: \(\frac{240}{380} = \frac{12}{19}\). On the Scientific tab, 240/380 and 12/19 both give about 0.632.

Choice C is correct. Choice D, \(\frac{4}{5}\), is the probability of an electric water heater given solar panels, the reversed condition. Choice A, \(\frac{240}{1{,}000}\), uses the whole town as the total, and choice B is the probability of no solar panels.
worked_example.verify:
N = 1000
both = Rational(80, 100)*Rational(30, 100)*N
heater = both + Rational(20, 100)*Rational(70, 100)*N
p = both/heater
assert p == Rational(12, 19) and value(choices[answer]) == p
assert all(value(choices[k]) != p for k in choices if k != answer)

lessons.title: Ratios, rates, proportions and units
lessons.what_is_tested: These questions ask you to work with quantities that change together at a constant rate: unit rates, proportions, ratios, scale drawings, and changing from one unit to another. On the Digital SAT they are mostly short word problems, sometimes with a table, and they are the base for many percent and data questions.
lessons.how_to_spot: Look for "per", "for every", "at this rate", "the ratio of … to …", a map or model scale, or a request for the answer in different units from the ones given.
method: Write down what is given and what is asked, with units (for example, miles and gallons give miles per gallon).
Find the unit rate (the amount for 1), or set up a proportion with the same units in the same places: \(\frac{a}{b} = \frac{c}{d}\).
For unit changes, multiply by conversion fractions equal to 1, arranged so that the unwanted units cancel.
Compute, then reread the question: does it ask for a total, one part, or a different unit?
Check the size: more time should mean more distance, and a bigger unit should mean a smaller number.
pitfalls: Flipping a rate (gallons per mile instead of miles per gallon) gives an answer that is far too small or too large.
Stopping at the unit rate when the question asks for a total.
With a part-to-part ratio such as 3 to 5, forgetting that the total is 8 parts.
Converting only one unit of a rate, such as meters to kilometers but not seconds to hours.
Scaling an area by the length scale factor instead of by its square.
lessons.calculator: Use the Scientific tab for chains of conversion factors, and type the whole chain as one expression so nothing is rounded halfway. Decide which way up each fraction goes from the units first; the calculator cannot do that for you.

cards.title: Foundations: unit rates and simple proportions
steps: Find what one unit is worth: for a rate, divide the amount by the number of units; for a ratio such as 3 to 5, divide the total by the number of parts, \(3 + 5 = 8\).
Multiply that one-unit value by the number of units you need.
Keep the units next to every number so you can see what each number means.
Check direction and size: more minutes should give more pages, a larger share should give more people.

worked_example.stem: A printer prints 132 pages in 4 minutes. At this rate, how many pages does the printer print in 7 minutes?
walkthrough: Unit rate: \(132 \div 4 = 33\) pages per minute.
Multiply by the new time: \(33 \times 7 = 231\) pages.
Check: 7 minutes is a bit less than twice 4 minutes, and 231 is a bit less than twice 132, so the answer is reasonable.
Choice C is correct. Choice A, 33, is the number of pages in one minute: it stops one step early. Choice D multiplies 132 by 4 instead of dividing, and choice B adds 7 to 132 instead of scaling.
worked_example.verify:
rate = Rational(132, 4)
assert rate == 33
assert value(choices[answer]) == rate*7 == 231
assert all(value(choices[k]) != 231 for k in choices if k != answer)

cards.title: Medium: rates with time and unit changes
steps: Decide what the question wants: a time, an amount or a rate, and in which unit.
Divide the amount by the rate to get a time, or multiply the rate by the time to get an amount.
Change units with one conversion: 60 minutes = 1 hour, 1,000 meters = 1 kilometer.
Reread the question and give the answer in the unit it asks for.

worked_example.stem: A water tanker in Karachi delivers water into a storage tank at a constant rate of 40 liters per minute. How many hours does it take the tanker to deliver 6,000 liters of water?
walkthrough: Time in minutes: \(6{,}000 \div 40 = 150\) minutes.
The question asks for hours: \(150 \div 60 = 2.5\) hours.
Enter 2.5 (or 5/2). Entering 150 gives the time in minutes, the wrong unit.
worked_example.verify:
minutes = Rational(6000, 40)
assert minutes == 150
hours = minutes/60
assert all(Rational(s) == hours == Rational(5, 2) for s in spr_answers)

cards.title: Advanced: converting rates with two units
steps: Write the starting rate as a fraction with both units, such as 6 meters over 1 second.
Multiply by conversion fractions equal to 1, arranged so each unwanted unit cancels (put seconds on top to cancel seconds on the bottom).
After the units cancel, multiply the numbers on top and divide by the numbers on the bottom.
Check the size: an hour is much longer than a second, and a kilometer is much longer than a meter.

worked_example.stem: A cyclist rides at a constant speed of 6 meters per second. What is the cyclist's speed, in kilometers per hour? (1 kilometer = 1,000 meters)
walkthrough: Seconds to hours: there are \(60 \times 60 = 3{,}600\) seconds in an hour, so \(6 \times 3{,}600 = 21{,}600\) meters per hour.
Meters to kilometers: \(21{,}600 \div 1{,}000 = 21.6\) kilometers per hour.
On the Scientific tab, type the whole chain at once: \(6 \times 3600 \div 1000\).

Choice B is correct. Choice A multiplies by 60 instead of 3,600, so it changes seconds only to minutes. Choice D, \(6 \times 60\), also uses minutes and never changes meters to kilometers, and choice C divides by 100 instead of 1,000.
worked_example.verify:
kmh = Rational(6)*3600/1000
assert kmh == Rational(108, 5)
assert value(choices[answer]) == kmh
assert all(value(choices[k]) != kmh for k in choices if k != answer)

cards.title: Challenge: scales for area and chained ratios
steps: Turn a scale into a length rule in useful units, for example 4 centimeters on the map represent 1 kilometer.
Change the lengths first, then compute the area or volume from the real lengths: an area scales by the square of the length scale, a volume by its cube.
For chained ratios (a to b and b to c), rewrite both so the shared quantity has the same number, then read a to c.
Check the units of the final answer, such as square kilometers rather than kilometers.

worked_example.stem: A map has a scale of 1 : 25,000, so 1 centimeter on the map represents 25,000 centimeters on the ground. A rectangular park is 4 centimeters long and 6 centimeters wide on the map. What is the actual area of the park, in square kilometers? (1 kilometer = 100,000 centimeters)
walkthrough: Actual length: \(4 \times 25{,}000 = 100{,}000\) centimeters, which is 1 kilometer.
Actual width: \(6 \times 25{,}000 = 150{,}000\) centimeters, which is 1.5 kilometers.
Area: \(1 \times 1.5 = 1.5\) square kilometers. Enter 1.5 (or 3/2).
Trap: multiplying the map area, 24 square centimeters, by 25,000 treats an area like a length. Area scales by \(25{,}000^{2}\), so change the lengths before you multiply.
worked_example.verify:
length = Rational(4*25000, 100000)
width = Rational(6*25000, 100000)
area = length*width
assert area == Rational(24)*25000**2/100000**2
assert all(Rational(s) == area == Rational(3, 2) for s in spr_answers)

lessons.title: Right triangles and trigonometry
lessons.what_is_tested: These questions use the Pythagorean theorem, the special right triangles (\(45^{\circ}\)-\(45^{\circ}\)-\(90^{\circ}\) and \(30^{\circ}\)-\(60^{\circ}\)-\(90^{\circ}\)) and the ratios sine, cosine and tangent to find missing sides or angles. Harder ones use the fact that \(\sin x^{\circ} = \cos(90 - x)^{\circ}\), model a context such as an angle of elevation, or find a ratio from partial information.
lessons.how_to_spot: A right triangle (marked with a small square or described in words) with two sides, or a side and an angle, given; or any \(\sin\), \(\cos\) or \(\tan\) in the question; or a context with a slope, ramp, ladder or angle of elevation.
method: Find the right angle; the side across from it is the hypotenuse, the longest side.
Label the other two sides opposite and adjacent, relative to the angle in the question.
Choose the tool: the Pythagorean theorem for three sides; a special right triangle for \(30^{\circ}\), \(45^{\circ}\) or \(60^{\circ}\) (both are on the reference sheet); SOH-CAH-TOA otherwise.
Set up the equation and solve; if only a ratio is known, write the sides as multiples of \(k\).
Check: the hypotenuse is the longest side, and every sine or cosine of an acute angle is between 0 and 1.
pitfalls: Labeling opposite and adjacent from the wrong angle, which turns \(\cos B\) into \(\cos A\) (wrong_quantity).
Inverting a ratio, for example taking \(\tan A\) as adjacent over opposite (reciprocal).
Adding the legs instead of their squares in \(a^{2} + b^{2} = c^{2}\), or forgetting the final square root (wrong_formula).
Putting \(x\sqrt{3}\) across from the \(30^{\circ}\) angle; the shortest side is across from \(30^{\circ}\) (concept).
Leaving the calculator in Rad mode when the angles are in degrees (arithmetic).
lessons.calculator: Use the Scientific tab for angles that are not special, such as \(40^{\circ}\): check that it is set to Deg, then evaluate \(\sin\), \(\cos\) or \(\tan\) directly. For \(30^{\circ}\), \(45^{\circ}\) and \(60^{\circ}\), the exact side patterns are faster and match answer choices written with radicals.

cards.title: Foundations: Pythagoras and SOH-CAH-TOA
steps: Mark the right angle and the hypotenuse across from it.
From the angle in the question, label the opposite side and the adjacent side.
Write the ratio (sine = opposite over hypotenuse, cosine = adjacent over hypotenuse, tangent = opposite over adjacent) or \(a^{2} + b^{2} = c^{2}\).
Substitute the side lengths and simplify.

worked_example.stem: In right triangle \(PQR\), what is the value of \(\tan P\)?
walkthrough: The right angle is at \(Q\), so the hypotenuse is \(\overline{PR} = 29\).
From angle \(P\), the opposite side is \(\overline{QR} = 21\) and the adjacent side is \(\overline{PQ} = 20\).
Tangent is opposite over adjacent: \(\tan P = \frac{21}{20}\), choice D.
Choice C, \(\frac{20}{21}\), is the reciprocal (adjacent over opposite), and choice B, \(\frac{21}{29}\), is \(\sin P\). Quick check of the labels: \(20^{2} + 21^{2} = 841 = 29^{2}\).
worked_example.verify:
P=figure['points']
d=lambda a,b: sqrt((P[a][0]-P[b][0])**2+(P[a][1]-P[b][1])**2)
ang=lambda a,v,b: N(acos(((P[a][0]-P[v][0])*(P[b][0]-P[v][0])+(P[a][1]-P[v][1])*(P[b][1]-P[v][1]))/(d(a,v)*d(b,v)))*180/pi)
assert P['Q'][0]==P['R'][0] and P['Q'][1]==P['P'][1]
opp=d('Q','R'); adj=d('P','Q'); hyp=d('P','R')
assert opp==21 and adj==20 and hyp==29
ans=opp/adj
assert value(choices[answer])==ans
assert all(value(choices[c])!=ans for c in choices if c!=answer)
assert value(choices['C'])==1/ans and value(choices['B'])==opp/hyp

cards.title: Medium: special right triangles and complements
steps: Spot a \(30^{\circ}\), \(45^{\circ}\) or \(60^{\circ}\) angle, or a square or equilateral triangle that splits into one.
Write the side pattern from the reference sheet: \(s, s, s\sqrt{2}\) or \(x, x\sqrt{3}, 2x\).
Find the multiplier from the side you know, then the side you need; for complementary angles use \(\sin x^{\circ} = \cos(90 - x)^{\circ}\).
Answer the question asked (a perimeter, a height) and check that the hypotenuse is the longest side.

worked_example.stem: The playing surface of a carrom board is a square. The diagonal of the playing surface is \(74\sqrt{2}\) centimeters long. What is the perimeter, in centimeters, of the playing surface?
walkthrough: The diagonal cuts the square into two \(45^{\circ}\)-\(45^{\circ}\)-\(90^{\circ}\) triangles, and the diagonal is their hypotenuse.
The reference sheet gives the sides of that triangle as \(s, s, s\sqrt{2}\). So \(s\sqrt{2} = 74\sqrt{2}\), and \(s = 74\).
The perimeter is \(4s = 4(74) = 296\) centimeters. Enter 296.
Stopping at \(s = 74\) answers a different question, and \(4 \cdot 74\sqrt{2}\) wrongly uses the diagonal as a side.
worked_example.verify:
s=symbols('s',positive=True)
ss=solve(Eq(s*sqrt(2),74*sqrt(2)),s)[0]
P=figure['points']
assert P['B'][0]-P['A'][0]==ss and P['C'][1]-P['B'][1]==ss and P['D'][1]-P['A'][1]==ss
assert Rational(spr_answers[0])==4*ss==296

cards.title: Advanced: trigonometry in context, with the calculator
steps: Draw the right triangle the context describes and mark the known angle and side.
Pick the ratio that links the side you know and the side you want, relative to that angle.
Solve for the unknown (for example, height \(= 30\tan 40^{\circ}\)); evaluate in the Scientific tab set to Deg, or use exact values for special angles.
Add any extra pieces the context includes (an eye or instrument height), then round as the question says.

worked_example.stem: A surveyor sets up an instrument on level ground 30 meters from the base of a vertical tower. The instrument's lens is 1.4 meters above the ground, and the angle of elevation from the lens to the top of the tower is \(40^{\circ}\), as shown. To the nearest tenth of a meter, what is the height of the tower?
walkthrough: The right triangle has vertices at the lens \(L\), the point \(Q\) on the tower at lens height, and the top \(T\). Its horizontal leg is \(LQ = 30\) meters, and the angle at \(L\) is \(40^{\circ}\).
\(QT\) is opposite the \(40^{\circ}\) angle and \(LQ\) is adjacent, so use tangent: \(\tan 40^{\circ} = \frac{QT}{30}\), which gives \(QT = 30\tan 40^{\circ}\).
In the Scientific tab, set to Deg, \(30\tan 40^{\circ} \approx 25.17\) meters.
Add the lens height: \(25.17 + 1.4 = 26.57\), which rounds to 26.6. Enter 26.6.
Forgetting the 1.4 meters gives 25.2. A negative result means the calculator was in Rad mode.
worked_example.verify:
P=figure['points']
d=lambda a,b: sqrt((P[a][0]-P[b][0])**2+(P[a][1]-P[b][1])**2)
ang=lambda a,v,b: N(acos(((P[a][0]-P[v][0])*(P[b][0]-P[v][0])+(P[a][1]-P[v][1])*(P[b][1]-P[v][1]))/(d(a,v)*d(b,v)))*180/pi)
h=Rational('1.4')+30*tan(40*pi/180)
assert abs(N(h)-Rational(spr_answers[0]))<0.05 and Rational(spr_answers[0])==Rational('26.6')
assert P['Q'][0]-P['L'][0]==30 and P['L'][0]==P['G'][0] and P['Q'][0]==P['F'][0]==P['T'][0]
assert abs(P['L'][1]-1.4)<1e-9 and abs(P['T'][1]-N(h))<0.01 and abs(ang('Q','L','T')-40)<0.1
assert abs(N(h-Rational('1.4'))-Rational('25.2'))<0.05

cards.title: Challenge: ratios with a multiplier
steps: Turn the given ratio (or a cofunction fact) into side lengths with a multiplier: \(\tan A = \frac{12}{5}\) means sides \(12k\) and \(5k\).
Use the Pythagorean theorem to write the third side in terms of \(k\); in a triangle without a right angle, draw an altitude first.
Use the extra fact (a perimeter, an area, one actual side) to find \(k\).
Compute the requested side or ratio and check it against the original ratio.

worked_example.stem: In right triangle \(ABC\), angle \(C\) is a right angle, \(\tan A = 2.4\), and the perimeter of the triangle is 60. What is the length of \(\overline{AC}\)?
walkthrough: \(\tan A = 2.4 = \frac{12}{5}\), so the leg opposite angle \(A\) is \(BC = 12k\) and the adjacent leg is \(AC = 5k\) for some \(k > 0\).
Pythagorean theorem: \(AB = \sqrt{(12k)^{2} + (5k)^{2}} = \sqrt{169k^{2}} = 13k\).
Choice D, 24, is \(BC\), the leg opposite angle \(A\), not the adjacent leg; choices B and C use the ratio numbers 12 and 13 without finding \(k\).
worked_example.verify:
k=symbols('k',positive=True)
ks=solve(Eq(12*k+5*k+sqrt((12*k)**2+(5*k)**2),60),k)
assert ks==[2] and Rational('2.4')==Rational(12,5)
ans=5*ks[0]
assert Rational(12*ks[0],ans)==Rational('2.4')
assert value(choices[answer])==ans==10
assert all(value(choices[c])!=ans for c in choices if c!=answer)
assert value(choices['D'])==12*ks[0]

lessons.title: Evaluating statistical claims
lessons.what_is_tested: You decide what a study's design allows you to conclude. Random selection from a population lets you generalize the results to that population; random assignment of treatments lets you conclude cause and effect. Without random assignment, you can claim only an association.
lessons.how_to_spot: The question describes how participants were chosen and how treatments were given, then asks for the most appropriate conclusion, the largest group the results apply to, or which design would allow a cause-and-effect claim.
method: Ask: were the participants selected at random from a larger population? If so, results generalize to that population, and no wider.
Ask: were the treatments assigned at random? If so, a cause-and-effect conclusion is possible.
If people chose their own treatment or were only observed, you can claim an association, never "causes".
Combine the two answers: cause and effect for a whole population needs both random selection and random assignment.
Check the exact group named in each choice: a state or a city, all employees or only app users, volunteers or everyone.
pitfalls: Saying "causes" for an observational study, even a large random one.
Generalizing to a bigger group than the one the sample came from.
Thinking volunteers rule out every conclusion: random assignment still supports cause and effect for the volunteers themselves.
Thinking a bigger sample fixes a design that has no random selection or no random assignment.

cards.title: Foundations: who do the results describe?
steps: Find the population the sample was randomly selected from.
The results apply to that population, not to a bigger or different group.
Rule out choices that are too wide (the whole country) or too narrow (only the people surveyed).
Check that the choice does not include people who had no chance to be selected.

worked_example.stem: A public library selected 300 of its members at random and asked whether they would use a new evening study room. Of those surveyed, \(70\%\) said they would. What is the largest group to which the results of the survey can appropriately be generalized?

choices.A: Only the 300 members who were surveyed
choices.B: All members of the public library
choices.C: All people who live in the library's city
choices.D: All members of every public library in the country

walkthrough: The 300 members were selected at random from the library's members, so the population is all members of the library.
Results from a random sample generalize to the population it was drawn from.

Choice B is correct. Choice C is too wide: people who are not members of the library had no chance to be selected. Choice A is too narrow, because random selection is exactly what lets the results describe all members.
worked_example.verify:
random_selection, population = True, 'All members of the public library'
assert random_selection
assert answer == 'B' and choices[answer] == population

cards.title: Medium: association or cause and effect?
steps: Check how the groups were formed: did the researchers assign the treatment at random, or did people choose or simply report?
Without random assignment, use words like "is associated with", never "causes".
Use random selection to decide which population the association describes.
Reject choices that claim cause, or that shrink or stretch the population.

worked_example.stem: Researchers selected 1,000 adults at random from a large city and asked each one how many minutes they walk on a typical day and how many hours they sleep on a typical night. Adults who walked at least 30 minutes a day slept longer, on average, than adults who walked less. Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?

choices.A: Walking at least 30 minutes a day causes adults in the city to sleep longer.
choices.B: Among adults in the city, walking at least 30 minutes a day is associated with sleeping longer.
choices.C: Walking at least 30 minutes a day causes all adults everywhere to sleep longer.
choices.D: No conclusion can be drawn about adults in the city, because the adults were not assigned to walk.

walkthrough: The adults were selected at random from the city, so the results describe adults in the city.
The researchers did not assign how much anyone walked; they only asked. So the study shows an association, not cause and effect.

Choice B is correct. Choice A is the strongest trap: adults who walk more may differ in other ways (age, work, health) that also affect sleep. Choice D goes too far the other way: random selection still lets you describe an association in the city's population.
worked_example.verify:
random_selection, random_assignment = True, False
assert random_selection and not random_assignment
assert answer == 'B' and 'associated with' in choices[answer] and 'in the city' in choices[answer]

cards.title: Advanced: reading a study design
steps: For each study, note two things: random selection from the population? Random assignment of treatments?
Random assignment only: cause and effect for the participants in the study.
Random selection only: an association that generalizes to the population.
Both: cause and effect that generalizes to the population. Neither: only an association among the participants.

worked_example.stem: Six studies tested whether a new study app improves vocabulary test scores among the students at a large university. The table shows whether each study selected its participants at random from all students at the university and whether it assigned the app to participants at random. For how many of the six studies can a cause-and-effect conclusion be generalized to all students at the university?
walkthrough: To generalize a cause-and-effect conclusion to all students, a study needs both random selection and random assignment.
Check each row: only studies III and V have Yes in both columns.
Enter 2.
Trap: counting every study with random assignment (II, III, V and VI) gives 4, but studies II and VI support cause and effect only for their own participants.
worked_example.verify:
rows = figure['rows']
both = [r[0] for r in rows if r[1] == 'Yes' and r[2] == 'Yes']
assert both == ['III', 'V']
assert [Rational(s) for s in spr_answers] == [len(both)]

cards.title: Challenge: the scope of a cause-and-effect conclusion
steps: Name the population the participants were randomly selected from; it may be a subgroup (one year group, one city, app users).
Check that the treatments were randomly assigned within the sample.
The cause-and-effect conclusion applies to that subgroup: not to everyone, and not only to the participants.
Reject choices that change the population or that claim more (or less) than the design allows.

worked_example.stem: A university has 12,000 students, and 3,000 of them are first-year students. Researchers selected 120 first-year students at random. They randomly assigned 60 of these students to attend a weekly study-skills workshop and the other 60 to not attend. At the end of the term, the students who attended the workshop had a higher average grade. Which of the following conclusions is best supported by the study?

choices.A: Attending the workshop causes higher grades for all students at the university.
choices.B: Attending the workshop likely causes higher grades for first-year students at the university.
choices.C: Attending the workshop likely caused higher grades only for the 60 students who attended it.
choices.D: No cause-and-effect conclusion can be drawn, because only first-year students were selected.

walkthrough: Random selection was from the 3,000 first-year students, so the population is the first-year students at the university.
The workshop was assigned at random, so a cause-and-effect conclusion is possible.
Together: attending the workshop likely causes higher grades for first-year students at this university. Choice B is correct.

Choice A is the strongest trap: students in other years had no chance to be selected, so the result cannot be stretched to all 12,000 students. Choice C is too narrow, because random selection lets the result reach all first-year students.
worked_example.verify:
population, random_selection, random_assignment = 3000, True, True
assert random_selection and random_assignment and population < 12000
assert answer == 'B' and 'first-year students at the university' in choices[answer]

lessons.title: Systems of two linear equations
lessons.what_is_tested: You find the pair \((x, y)\) that makes two linear equations true at the same time, set up a system from a word problem, and decide when a system has no solution or infinitely many. On a graph, the solution is the point where the two lines cross.
lessons.how_to_spot: Two equations are stacked together, or a story gives two facts about two unknown amounts (a total count and a total cost, or two different purchases). The question asks for \(x\), \(y\), a combination such as \(x + y\), or the number of solutions.
method: Name the two unknowns and write one equation for each fact.
If one equation is already solved for a variable, substitute that expression into the other equation.
Otherwise, multiply one or both equations so a variable has the same coefficient, then subtract (or add opposites) to eliminate it.
Solve for the remaining variable, then substitute back to find the other one.
Give exactly what is asked; sometimes adding or subtracting the equations gives it directly.
pitfalls: Choosing a pair that makes only one of the two equations true (concept).
Reporting \(y\) when the question asks for \(x\), or reversing the order of the pair (wrong_quantity).
Multiplying only one side or one term of an equation before eliminating (arithmetic).
Subtracting equations without subtracting every term, especially negative ones (sign_error).
Mixing up the special cases: parallel lines (same slope, different intercepts) mean no solution; the same line means infinitely many (concept).
lessons.calculator: On the Graph tab, type both equations exactly as given and tap the intersection point; this is often the fastest route when the numbers are decimals or fractions. Systems with small whole numbers are usually just as fast by elimination.

cards.title: Foundations: substitution
steps: Find the equation that is already solved for one variable, such as \(y = x + 4\).
Substitute that expression into the other equation.
Solve for the variable that is left, then substitute back to find the other.
Check the pair in both equations before you choose.

worked_example.stem: \[y = x + 4\] \[2x + y = 19\] What is the solution \((x, y)\) to the system of equations above?
walkthrough: The first equation gives \(y\) directly: \(y = x + 4\).
Substitute into the second: \(2x + (x + 4) = 19\), so \(3x + 4 = 19\) and \(3x = 15\).
So \(x = 5\) and \(y = 5 + 4 = 9\). The solution is \((5, 9)\), choice D.
Check both: \(9 = 5 + 4\) and \(2(5) + 9 = 19\). Choice B makes the second equation true but not the first (\(7 \ne 6 + 4\)), and choice C reverses the coordinates.
worked_example.verify:
x, y = symbols('x y')
sol = solve([Eq(y, x + 4), Eq(2*x + y, 19)], [x, y])
assert sol == {x: 5, y: 9}
pt = lambda s: [value(t) for t in s.strip('\\()').split(',')]
assert pt(choices[answer]) == [5, 9]
assert all(pt(choices[k]) != [5, 9] for k in choices if k != answer)

cards.title: Medium: elimination in a word problem
steps: Write one equation for each purchase or fact, using the same letters in both.
Multiply one equation so that one variable has the same coefficient in both.
Subtract to eliminate that variable, then solve for the one that is left.
Make sure the value you give is the one the question asks about.

worked_example.stem: A sports shop in Islamabad sells cricket balls and rolls of bat grip tape, each at a fixed price. Hira pays 1,240 rupees for 3 cricket balls and 2 rolls of grip tape. Bilal pays 1,080 rupees for 1 cricket ball and 4 rolls of grip tape. What is the price, in rupees, of 1 roll of grip tape?
walkthrough: Let \(b\) be the price of a ball and \(g\) the price of a roll of tape: \(3b + 2g = 1{,}240\) and \(b + 4g = 1{,}080\).
Multiply the second equation by 3: \(3b + 12g = 3{,}240\).
Subtract the first equation from this one: \(10g = 2{,}000\), so \(g = 200\).
The question asks for the tape, so enter 200. The ball costs \(1{,}080 - 4(200) = 280\) rupees; entering 280 answers the wrong question.
worked_example.verify:
b, g = symbols('b g')
s = solve([Eq(3*b + 2*g, 1240), Eq(b + 4*g, 1080)], [b, g])
assert s == {b: 280, g: 200}
assert [Rational(v) for v in spr_answers] == [s[g]]

cards.title: Advanced: decimals, graphs and combinations
steps: Turn a graph or table into equations (slope and intercept), or use the equations given.
Solve by substitution or elimination, or graph both equations on the Graph tab and read the intersection.
Check the coordinates in both equations.
Compute the combination the question asks for, such as \(x + y\).

worked_example.stem: \[3x + 2y = 7\] \[y = 0.5x - 4.5\] If \((x, y)\) is the solution to the system of equations above, what is the value of \(x + y\)?
walkthrough: Calculator route (Graph tab): type \(3x + 2y = 7\) and \(y = 0.5x - 4.5\); the lines meet at \((4, -2.5)\).
By hand: substitute into the first equation: \(3x + 2(0.5x - 4.5) = 7\), so \(3x + x - 9 = 7\), \(4x = 16\) and \(x = 4\).
So \(x + y = 4 + (-2.5) = 1.5\), choice B. Choice C is \(x\) alone, choice A is \(y\) alone, and choice D is \(x - y\).
worked_example.verify:
x, y = symbols('x y')
s = solve([Eq(3*x + 2*y, 7), Eq(y, Rational(1, 2)*x - Rational(9, 2))], [x, y])
assert s == {x: 4, y: Rational(-5, 2)}
t = s[x] + s[y]
assert value(choices[answer]) == t == Rational(3, 2)
assert all(value(choices[k]) != t for k in choices if k != answer)

cards.title: Challenge: no solution or infinitely many
steps: Write both equations in the form \(Ax + By = C\).
Find the number that turns one equation's known coefficient into the other's (for example, \(3y\) into \(6y\) means times 2).
Infinitely many solutions: that same multiple also matches the other coefficient and the constant. No solution: the left sides match but the constants do not.
Solve the small equations for the constants, then answer the question.

worked_example.stem: \[ax + 3y = 12\] \[4x + 6y = b\] In the system of equations above, \(a\) and \(b\) are constants. If the system has infinitely many solutions, what is the value of \(a + b\)?
walkthrough: Infinitely many solutions means the two equations describe the same line, so one equation is a multiple of the other.
Compare the \(y\)-terms: \(6y = 2 \cdot 3y\), so the second equation must be 2 times the first: \(2ax + 6y = 24\).
Match it with \(4x + 6y = b\): \(2a = 4\), so \(a = 2\), and \(b = 24\).

So \(a + b = 26\). If \(a = 2\) but \(b\) were not 24, the lines would be parallel and the system would have no solution; a student who stops at \(b = 12\) (forgetting to double the constant) gets 14.
worked_example.verify:
a, b, k = symbols('a b k')
s = solve([Eq(k*a, 4), Eq(k*3, 6), Eq(k*12, b)], [a, b, k], dict=True)
assert s == [{a: 2, b: 24, k: 2}]
assert [Rational(v) for v in spr_answers] == [s[0][a] + s[0][b]]

lessons.title: Two-variable data and models
lessons.what_is_tested: You read scatterplots and tables that relate two quantities, use a line of best fit to make predictions, interpret its slope and intercept, and decide whether a linear or an exponential model fits. Harder questions build a model from two points or compare two models.
lessons.how_to_spot: A scatterplot, a line or curve of best fit, a table of x- and y-values, or words such as "predicted", "model", "line of best fit" or "by the same percent".
method: Identify \(x\) and \(y\) and their units from the axis labels or column headings.
To predict, substitute the x-value into the equation of the line (or curve) of best fit.
Slope: the change in predicted \(y\) for each increase of 1 in \(x\). The y-intercept is the predicted \(y\) when \(x = 0\).
Residual: actual y-value minus predicted y-value (positive when the point is above the line).
Linear data change by the same amount at each equal step; exponential data change by the same factor at each equal step.
pitfalls: Mixing up the slope and the y-intercept when interpreting a model.
Reading a data point instead of the line when the question asks for a predicted value.
Calling data exponential or linear without checking the differences and the ratios.
Using the change for 1 unit when the question asks about a change of several units.
lessons.calculator: On the Graph tab, enter the model's equation and the vertical line for the x-value you need (for example \(x = 15\)); the intersection listed below the graph gives the prediction. To compare two models, enter both and read their intersections.

cards.title: Foundations: predictions from a line of best fit
steps: Read the axis labels: what are \(x\) and \(y\), and in which units?
Find the x-value the question gives.
Substitute it into the equation of the line of best fit and compute \(y\).
Check that your answer is close to the plotted points with similar x-values.

worked_example.stem: The scatterplot shows the number of rainy days \(x\) in a month and the number of umbrellas \(y\) sold that month at a shop in Colombo, Sri Lanka, for 10 months. The line of best fit is shown and has the equation \(y = 12x + 20\). Based on the line of best fit, how many umbrellas are predicted to be sold in a month with 15 rainy days?
walkthrough: \(x\) is the number of rainy days and \(y\) is the number of umbrellas sold.
Check: the months with 14 and 17 rainy days had 186 and 226 umbrellas sold, and 200 lies between them.
Choice D is correct. Choice C, 180, forgets to add the intercept, 20. Choice A is only the slope, and choice B adds 15 and 20.
worked_example.verify:
x = symbols('x')
pred = sympify(figure['line']).subs(x, 15)
assert pred == 200
assert value(choices[answer]) == pred
assert all(value(choices[k]) != pred for k in choices if k != answer)

cards.title: Medium: linear or exponential? Read the table
steps: Find the differences between consecutive y-values (for equal steps in \(x\)).
If the differences are equal, the model is linear: \(y = b + mx\).
If not, divide consecutive y-values; equal ratios mean exponential, \(y = a(r)^{x}\), where \(a\) is the value at \(x = 0\).
Test your equation on two rows, including one where \(x\) is not 0.

worked_example.stem: The table shows the value \(y\), in dollars, of a laptop \(x\) years after it was bought. Which equation models the data in the table?
walkthrough: Differences: \(720 - 900 = -180\) and \(576 - 720 = -144\). They are not equal, so the model is not linear.
Ratios: \(\frac{720}{900} = \frac{576}{720} = \frac{460.80}{576} = 0.8\). Equal ratios mean exponential decay with factor 0.8 (the laptop keeps \(80\%\) of its value each year).

Choice B is correct. Choice A fits only the first two rows (it gives 540 at \(x = 2\)). Choice C uses the part lost each year, 0.2, instead of the part kept, 0.8, and choice D starts from the year-1 value.
worked_example.verify:
x = symbols('x')
rows = [(Integer(a), Rational(b)) for a, b in figure['rows']]
fits = lambda k: all(value(choices[k].replace('y = ', '')).subs(x, a) == b for a, b in rows)
assert fits(answer)
assert not any(fits(k) for k in choices if k != answer)

cards.title: Advanced: slope and predictions from two points on the line
steps: Use two points that lie on the line of best fit (they are often given in the stem).
Slope = change in \(y\) ÷ change in \(x\); keep its sign.
Write the line as \(y = y_{1} + m(x - x_{1})\), or find its y-intercept.
Answer exactly what is asked: a prediction, a change over several units (slope × number of units), or a residual.

worked_example.stem: The scatterplot shows the ticket price \(x\), in dollars, and the number of tickets sold \(y\), in hundreds, for 8 concerts at a theater. The line of best fit passes through the points \((10, 42)\) and \((30, 27)\). According to the line of best fit, how many hundred tickets would be sold for a concert with a ticket price of 50 dollars?
walkthrough: Slope: \(\frac{27 - 42}{30 - 10} = \frac{-15}{20} = -0.75\), so the predicted sales drop by 0.75 hundred tickets for each dollar.
To check on the Graph tab, enter \(y = 42 - 0.75(x - 10)\) and \(x = 50\); the intersection listed below the graph is \((50, 12)\). Trap: dropping the minus sign of the slope gives \(42 + 30 = 72\).
worked_example.verify:
x = symbols('x')
m = Rational(27 - 42, 30 - 10)
line = 42 + m*(x - 10)
assert simplify(line - sympify(figure['line'], rational=True)) == 0
assert [Rational(s) for s in spr_answers] == [line.subs(x, 50)] == [12]

cards.title: Challenge: building an exponential model from two points
steps: Write the model \(f(t) = a(b)^{t}\) and substitute the two given points to get two equations.
Divide one equation by the other so that \(a\) cancels, then solve for \(b\).
Substitute \(b\) back to find \(a\), which is the value at \(t = 0\).
To compare with a linear model, evaluate both at whole-number values of \(t\), or enter both on the Graph tab and read their intersection.

worked_example.stem: A cooking channel's number of followers is modeled by \(f(t) = a(b)^{t}\), where \(f(t)\) is the number of followers, in thousands, \(t\) months after the chef began posting a video every day, and \(a\) and \(b\) are positive constants. The model gives 6 thousand followers when \(t = 1\) and 13.5 thousand followers when \(t = 3\). According to the model, how many thousand followers did the channel have when the chef began posting a video every day?
walkthrough: Substitute the two points: \(ab = 6\) and \(ab^{3} = 13.5\).
Divide the second equation by the first: \(b^{2} = \frac{13.5}{6} = 2.25\), so \(b = 1.5\) (\(b\) is positive).
Then \(a = \frac{6}{1.5} = 4\), and \(f(0) = a = 4\) thousand followers. Check: \(4(1.5)^{3} = 13.5\).
Choice B is correct. Choice A assumes linear growth of 3.75 thousand per month. Choice D divides 6 by \(b^{2}\) instead of \(b\), and choice C is the value at \(t = 1\), not at \(t = 0\).
worked_example.verify:
a, b = symbols('a b', positive=True)
sol = solve([Eq(a*b, 6), Eq(a*b**3, Rational(27, 2))], [a, b], dict=True)
assert len(sol) == 1 and sol[0][b] == Rational(3, 2)
assert value(choices[answer]) == sol[0][a] == 4
assert all(value(choices[k]) != 4 for k in choices if k != answer)
